outcome=$(jq -r '.outcome // "error"' <<<"$report")
case "$code:$outcome" in
  0:verified)
    if jq -e '[.rejected[]? | select(.outcome == "verification-failed")] | length > 0' <<<"$report" >/dev/null; then
      ./notify-security.sh "$report" # a rejected candidate failed verification
    fi
    echo "reusing $(jq -r .reference <<<"$report") (result: $(jq -r .result <<<"$report"))"
    [ "$(jq -r .result <<<"$report")" = passed ] || exit 1
    ;;
  4:miss)
    echo "no attestation for $(jq -r .fingerprint <<<"$report"), running test"
    ./run-tests.sh
    ;;
  5:verification-failed)
    echo "::error::untrusted attestation for $(jq -r .testId <<<"$report"): $(jq -r .reason <<<"$report")"
    ./notify-security.sh "$report"
    ./run-tests.sh
    ;;
  *)
    echo "aval could not decide (exit $code), running test"
    ./run-tests.sh
    ;;
esac

Check both the exit code and outcome; if they disagree, treat it as error. The policy file format (--policy) is described in trust-model.md.

docs.title: Guidance for consumers
docs.text:
• Always verify. Parse and Validate only check structure. A parsed predicate is a claim, not evidence. runner.identity inside the predicate is self-reported; the authoritative identity is the verified signer.
  • Treat verification-failed as a security event. Log it, alert on it, never fold it into "miss" or silently re-run without a trace.
  • Fail closed. Any outcome other than verified means run the test.
  • Consume by digest. Tags are only for lookup.
  • Pin versions. Check schemaVersion == "v2" on predicates (Validate does this) and version == "aval.trianalab.io/verify-report/v1" on reports. Reject versions you do not know. Within a version, ignore unknown fields: changes are additive.
  • Respect cacheability. non-deterministic results are never reusable; do not widen that in your adapter.

docs.title: Example: Pacto as an external consumer
docs.text:
This is a conceptual example of an integration that lives outside Aval. Aval does not import or depend on Pacto and knows nothing about Pacto concepts.

Pacto could consume Aval results through pkg/evidence or aval verify --output json: verify the attestation, convert the verified predicate into Pacto's own typed evidence, and evaluate Pacto's own requirements against it. That adapter lives in Pacto's repository, never in Aval. Aval will not grow Pacto-specific fields; any metadata Pacto (or any other tool) needs to carry goes in annotations, using reverse-DNS keys (for example dev.pacto.service). Aval never interprets annotations.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Go from an empty folder to a reused, verified test result in five minutes. You will see the four things Aval does: a miss, a reuse, a changed input and a rejected attestation.

You need aval (Install, one line), Docker and openssl. Copy each block into one shell, in order. The text block under it is what you should see. ... stands for a digest that is different on every run.

docs.title: 1. Start a registry
docs.text:
Aval keeps results in an OCI registry. Start one on your laptop. Port 5001, because macOS uses 5000 for AirPlay:

docker run -d --name aval-registry -p 5001:5000 registry:2

docs.title: 2. Make a project
docs.text:
One input file and a contract, aval.yaml. The contract names the test command and the files it reads (scope). Aval hashes those files into a fingerprint:

mkdir aval-demo && cd aval-demo
mkdir src && echo hello > src/hello.txt
cat > aval.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Test
metadata:
  name: hello
runner:
  command: ["grep", "-q", "hello", "src/hello.txt"]
scope:
  source: ["src/**"]
cacheability: hermetic
EOF

docs.title: 3. Make a key and a policy
docs.text:
The key signs your results. The policy says which signers you trust. Aval accepts ECDSA P-256 keys:

openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out aval.key
openssl pkey -in aval.key -pubout -out aval.pub
cat > policy.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Policy
minTrustLevel: developer
identities:
  - publicKey: aval.pub
    trustLevel: developer
EOF

docs.title: 4. First run: a miss
docs.text:
No result exists for these inputs, so the test runs. Aval signs the passing result with aval.key and pushes it:

aval run --push --key aval.key --registry localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval

test hello fingerprint sha256:fb3906f246f9255cf129e24de1256ac47b85e33cc548f3f517e94e237db0de06
miss hello sha256:fb3906f246f9255cf129e24de1256ac47b85e33cc548f3f517e94e237db0de06
reason: no trust policy configured: pass --policy to reuse verified results
ran hello: passed (exit 0)
pushed localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval@sha256:...

docs.title: 5. Second run: a reuse
docs.text:
Check that a result you trust exists for these exact inputs:

aval verify --registry localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval --policy policy.yaml
echo "exit code: $?"

verified hello sha256:fb3906f246f9255cf129e24de1256ac47b85e33cc548f3f517e94e237db0de06
signer: key ..., trust level developer
reference: localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval@sha256:...
exit code: 0

Run again. Aval finds the verified result and skips the test:

aval run --registry localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval --policy policy.yaml

test hello fingerprint sha256:fb3906f246f9255cf129e24de1256ac47b85e33cc548f3f517e94e237db0de06
verified hello sha256:fb3906f246f9255cf129e24de1256ac47b85e33cc548f3f517e94e237db0de06
signer: key ..., trust level developer
reference: localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval@sha256:...
reused passed result

docs.title: 6. Change an input: a miss again
docs.text:
Edit a file in scope. The fingerprint changes, no result matches it, and the test runs:

echo "hello, world" > src/hello.txt
aval run --registry localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval --policy policy.yaml

test hello fingerprint sha256:d52167b48089d3c3add62a6e81c6bfb0aa8d90baa98a69235c48bd892297170b
miss hello sha256:d52167b48089d3c3add62a6e81c6bfb0aa8d90baa98a69235c48bd892297170b
reason: localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval: no attestation found for fingerprint
ran hello: passed (exit 0)

docs.title: 7. A result from an untrusted signer: exit 5
docs.text:
Someone who can push to the registry, but has a key your policy does not trust, publishes a passing result for the new inputs. Aval rejects it, runs the test anyway and exits 5. Exit 5 is a security event, not a miss. Changing the bytes of a signed result breaks its signature and ends the same way:

openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out other.key
aval run --push --key other.key --registry localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval
aval run --registry localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval --policy policy.yaml
echo "exit code: $?"

test hello fingerprint sha256:d52167b48089d3c3add62a6e81c6bfb0aa8d90baa98a69235c48bd892297170b
miss hello sha256:d52167b48089d3c3add62a6e81c6bfb0aa8d90baa98a69235c48bd892297170b
reason: no trust policy configured: pass --policy to reuse verified results
ran hello: passed (exit 0)
pushed localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval@sha256:...
test hello fingerprint sha256:d52167b48089d3c3add62a6e81c6bfb0aa8d90baa98a69235c48bd892297170b
aval: SECURITY: 1 attestation(s) for hello failed signature or policy verification; treat it as a security event, see https://github.com/TrianaLab/aval/blob/main/docs/trust-model.md
verification-failed hello sha256:d52167b48089d3c3add62a6e81c6bfb0aa8d90baa98a69235c48bd892297170b
reference: localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval@sha256:...
reason: attestation verification failed: signature: signer key id "..." is not in the trust policy (trust policy policy.yaml)
ran hello: passed (exit 0)
exit code: 5

docs.title: What just happened
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  files[src/hello.txt<br>listed in scope] --> fp[fingerprint<br>sha256:fb39...]
  fp --> look{result for this<br>fingerprint?}
  look -- no --> miss([miss: run the test,<br>sign and push<br>steps 4 and 6]):::muted
  look -- "yes, signer in policy.yaml" --> ok([verified: reuse,<br>skip the test<br>step 5]):::ok
  look -- "yes, only untrusted signers" --> bad([verification-failed:<br>run the test, exit 5<br>step 7]):::err
  • The fingerprint covers only what scope lists. Change one byte there and it is a new fingerprint (step 6).
  • A result is reused only if its signer is in your policy (step 5). A result from any other signer is reported as a security event. If no trusted result exists, the test runs and Aval exits 5 (step 7).
  • When Aval cannot prove a result is safe to reuse, the test runs.

Stop the registry when you are done:

docker rm -f aval-registry

Next: the test contract for real scopes, the trust model for keyless signing in CI, and the CLI reference for every exit code.

docs.title: Trust model
docs.text:
Status: pre-alpha. Milestone 1 (contract + fingerprint) is implemented. Signing (attest.Sign), push, lookup and fetch (internal/registry), verification (evidence.Verify, attest.Verifier) and the policy file (policy.Load) are implemented; aval verify, aval run and aval push use them. This document describes the model the code is built around; where behavior is not implemented yet, it says so.

The predicate type, media types and the aval.trianalab.io/v1 apiVersion are frozen; see artifact-format.md.

docs.title: What a signature proves
docs.text:
An Aval attestation is a DSSE envelope around an in-toto Statement whose predicate (evidence.Predicate) says: "test test.id, with inputs hashing to execution.fingerprint, produced result on subject".

A valid signature proves:

  • Who claims it. The signer identity (OIDC issuer + certificate subject for keyless, or a key) is bound to the claim.
  • Integrity of the claim. The predicate has not been modified since it was signed.

A valid signature does not prove:

  • that the test actually ran;
  • that it ran honestly (unmodified test code, no skipped cases, no patched runner);
  • that inputs not declared in aval.yaml were the same. The fingerprint only covers what the contract declares (see contract.md). Anything else is invisible to Aval.

So reuse is never "the signature is valid". It is "the signature is valid, the signer is someone the policy trusts at a sufficient level, and the fingerprint and test id match what we computed locally".

runner.identity, runner.issuer and runner.trustLevel inside the predicate are what the signer claims. The authoritative identity is the verified signer, and the trust level is the one the policy grants to that signer, not the one written in the predicate. In code: attest.Verifier verifies the Sigstore bundle and returns the evidence.Signer it binds (the OIDC issuer and subject of the Fulcio certificate, or the key's id), and evidence.Verify looks that signer up in the policy's Identities with evidence.MatchSigner. A key-based signer only matches identities that list its public key; a keyless one only matches issuer and subject entries.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text:
attest.Sign (sigstore-go) signs the in-toto statement as a DSSE envelope in one of two modes:

  • Keyless (CI): an ephemeral key, a short-lived Fulcio certificate for the OIDC token the caller passes in, and a Rekor entry (always recorded, since the certificate expires in minutes and Rekor's timestamp is what makes it verifiable later). Signing always uses the Sigstore public-good instance (https://fulcio.sigstore.dev, https://rekor.sigstore.dev); the endpoints cannot be configured (TODO(milestone-5): signing against a private Sigstore deployment; verification already accepts its pinned trustedRoot). Obtaining the OIDC token is the caller's job, so no CI vendor or issuer is assumed.
  • Key-based (local): an unencrypted ECDSA P-256 PEM key (PKCS#8 or SEC1), for example from openssl ecparam -name prime256v1 -genkey -noout -out aval.key. Cosign keys are encrypted and not supported. No Rekor entry. The bundle's key hint is the key's evidence.PublicKeyID. Expect policies to grant such signatures at most level 1.

Besides the envelope, Sign returns the Sigstore bundle (v0.3 JSON) with the verification material (certificate or key hint, Rekor entry). registry.Push requires it and stores it next to the envelope as the second layer of the execution manifest (see artifact-format.md).

docs.title: Trust levels
docs.text:
evidence.TrustLevel, higher is stronger:

Level Name Constant Who Good for 0 unknown TrustUnknown level could not be established never accepted 1 developer TrustDeveloper a developer's local signature personal acceleration only: skip a test you already ran on your machine. Not full trust. 2 runner TrustRunner a CI runner with a verifiable workload identity (e.g. GitHub Actions OIDC) reuse in CI. CI should require at least this level. 3 isolated TrustIsolated an isolated execution with a verifiable attestation of the environment itself reuse where the runner host is not trusted either

Level 1 exists because a local signature is still useful to its author. Expect many security policies to refuse it outright; that is the intended use of MinTrustLevel.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
The trust policy decides which signers are accepted and at what level. It is policy.Policy (internal/policy), converted to evidence.VerifyOptions for evidence.Verify:

Field Meaning Identities accepted signers. Each evidence.Identity is either an OIDC Issuer plus a SubjectRegexp matched against the whole certificate subject (SAN), or a PublicKey, and the TrustLevel that signer is granted. Empty means nothing is accepted. MinTrustLevel minimum granted level required for reuse. Level 0 (unknown) and levels above 3 are never accepted, whatever this says. AllowedCacheability cacheability classes that may be reused besides hermetic and controlled-environment. Only external-dependencies has an effect; non-deterministic is never reusable. TrustedRoot Sigstore trusted root for keyless signatures (policy file only). ExpectedFingerprint, ExpectedTestID set by Aval from the local contract, not by the policy file. Must equal the predicate's execution.fingerprint and test.id. Required.

evidence.Verify checks, in order: the signature (through VerifyOptions.Signature), that the signer matches an accepted identity, that the granted level is at least MinTrustLevel, that the payload is an Aval in-toto statement whose subject equals the predicate's, the predicate structure, the expected fingerprint and test id, and the cacheability. Any failure is a *VerificationError (ErrVerification). The verified Signer is the policy entry that matched, plus the subject or keyId the signature actually carried, so the verify report shows who really signed.

The CLI (aval verify, aval run) checks the minimum level last instead: it calls evidence.Verify with MinTrustLevel developer, then checks the signed cacheability against the contract, then the policy's minTrustLevel. An attestation that passes every other check but whose signer the policy lists below minTrustLevel is routine non-reuse, like a developer result under a CI policy: outcome miss (exit 4), listed in rejected with outcome miss, never reused and never a security event. Any other failure, including a false claim from such a signer, is verification-failed (exit 5). Library callers of evidence.Verify still get ErrVerification for a level below MinTrustLevel.

attest.Verifier checks signatures with sigstore-go against the Sigstore bundle stored next to the envelope. A keyless signature must chain to a Fulcio CA in the trusted root, carry an embedded SCT from a trusted CT log, have a Rekor entry, and have a trusted timestamp (Rekor or a TSA) inside the certificate's validity. A key-based signature must verify with one of the policy's public keys; no Rekor entry is required. The envelope must be byte-for-byte the one the bundle signs. An attestation without a bundle never verifies.

Without --policy nothing is trusted. Aval does not even query the registry: the outcome is miss (exit 4) with the reason "no trust policy configured", and the test runs. This avoids reporting every attestation it finds as a verification failure just because no policy exists. Once a policy is configured, an attestation from a signer it does not list is a verification failure (exit 5); one from a signer it lists below minTrustLevel is a miss (exit 4). A policy file that cannot be loaded is outcome error (exit 1): the test runs and nothing is looked up. The trusted root is loaded only when a candidate's Sigstore bundle carries a certificate (a key-based bundle never needs it), at most once per command; if it cannot be loaded, that candidate is outcome error (exit 1, the test runs), never a verification failure.

docs.title: Policy file
docs.text:
apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Policy
minTrustLevel: runner           # developer | runner | isolated
# trustedRoot: sigstore/trusted_root.json  # keyless only; default: Sigstore public-good, fetched with TUF
identities:
  - issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
    subjectRegexp: https://github\.com/acme/orders/\.github/workflows/ci\.yaml@refs/heads/main
    trustLevel: runner
  - publicKey: keys/alice.pub   # PEM public key file
    trustLevel: developer
allowedCacheability: [external-dependencies]

policy.Load rejects, rather than ignores: unknown fields, more than one YAML document, another apiVersion or kind, a missing or unknown minTrustLevel or trustLevel (levels are written by name), no identities, an identity with both publicKey and issuer/subjectRegexp or with neither, a subjectRegexp that does not compile alone and anchored, a publicKey file that is not a PEM public key, and non-deterministic or an unknown class in allowedCacheability. Relative trustedRoot and publicKey paths are resolved against the policy file's directory.

docs.title: Keyless verification needs the network and a writable HOME
docs.text:
A policy with an issuer identity and no trustedRoot uses the Sigstore public-good trusted root. sigstore-go fetches it with TUF from tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev and caches it under $HOME/.sigstore. Aval loads it only when a candidate's Sigstore bundle carries a certificate, at most once per command. A miss or a key-based attestation never fetches it. Without network access, or with a HOME that cannot be written, the trusted root does not load: that candidate is outcome error (exit 1, never verification-failed), and aval run runs the test. Reuse is lost, never faked.

To avoid the dependency, pin the trusted root in the policy:

  1. Get trusted_root.json once, on a machine with network access. After one keyless aval verify there, sigstore-go has it at $HOME/.sigstore/root/tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev/targets/trusted_root.json.
  2. Commit it next to the policy and set trustedRoot: trusted_root.json (relative to the policy file).
  3. Refresh it when Sigstore rotates keys: a stale root fails to verify new certificates (outcome verification-failed), so watch for that after a Sigstore announcement.

Policies with only publicKey identities never fetch anything.

docs.title: Fail closed
docs.text:
If Aval cannot prove that a previous execution is equivalent and trusted, the test runs.

  • Fingerprint errors (empty source scope, missing or mismatched dependency, symlink in scope, unreadable file): input equivalence cannot be proven, so there is nothing to look up. Run the test.
  • Registry errors (unreachable, auth failure): outcome error, exit 1. For execution purposes this is a miss: run the test. A malformed attestation manifest, or a fingerprint tag that does not point at the fingerprint anchor, is a verification failure (exit 5).
  • Consume by digest. registry.Lookup resolves the tag sha256-<fingerprint hex>, checks that it points at the fingerprint's deterministic anchor manifest (a moved tag is a verification failure), and returns the anchor's referrers as candidate manifest digests; everything after that (fetch, verify, report reference) uses repo@sha256:.... The tag is only an index for lookup. It is mutable and is never trusted on its own.
  • No silent replacement. Pushes only add referrers to the anchor; a later push for the same fingerprint cannot replace an earlier attestation. Every candidate is verified and the policy picks the verified one with the highest trust level. A candidate that fails verification never decides the outcome while another verifies, and is listed in rejected in the verify report (and stderr gets one aval: SECURITY: ... line), so the security event stays visible. A candidate that cannot be fetched or checked blocks reuse (the test runs), because it might have outranked the verified one.
  • Unknown or missing fields in aval.yaml are rejected (exit 2) rather than ignored.

aval run --no-reuse always runs and never looks anything up.

docs.title: What aval run does with each outcome
docs.text:
aval run makes the same decision as aval verify and prints it as the verify text report (--report <file> also writes the JSON report). Only verified reuses; everything else runs runner.command in the contract's directory:

Lookup outcome aval run verified, result passed reuse, do not run verified, result failed reuse the failure, do not run miss (also: no --registry, no --policy, --no-reuse, non-deterministic, external-dependencies not in AllowedCacheability, only signers below minTrustLevel) run error (registry, policy or fingerprint error) run verification-failed run, print aval: SECURITY: ... on stderr

The exit codes, from the CLI reference:

Code aval run aval verify aval push 0 the test passed, or a verified passing result was reused a verified result exists (passing or failing) pushed 1 error (the test still runs when it can), or a false hit in --shadow error: registry, policy, trusted root or fingerprint error: signing, registry or a result that does not match the current inputs 2 bad flags or invalid aval.yaml bad flags or invalid aval.yaml bad flags or invalid aval.yaml 3 the test failed, or a verified failing result was reused not used not used 4 not used: a miss runs the test miss: no result the policy can reuse not used 5 verification failed, after running the test: a security event verification failed: a security event not used 6 reserved, never returned reserved, never returned reserved, never returned

A miss (4) is routine. A verification failure (5) means someone published a result the policy does not trust; never hide it or retry it away.

A fingerprint error leaves nothing to look up or record: the test runs, the report has outcome error with the reason, and --push fails (exit 1). Otherwise the run is recorded as an unsigned predicate in --result (default .aval/result.json) and, with --push, signed and published. aval push publishes a recorded result later, only if its test id, cacheability and fingerprint still match the contract.

A --report file that cannot be written does not skip the test: aval run then never reuses, runs the test, and still exits 5 on a verification failure.

$SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN is read once and removed from the environment before runner.command starts: the code under test cannot use it to sign results as the workload identity.

Reasons can carry text from an untrusted attestation, so the text output and stderr escape newlines, control and other non-printable characters and invalid UTF-8 with Go escapes (\n, \x1b, \u2028); quotes and backslashes stay as they are. Such text never starts a line of its own (a CI log command, a terminal escape). The JSON report keeps the reason as is.

Each command prints the reason once, in the report: stderr does not repeat it. On a verification failure stderr gets a single aval: SECURITY: ... line that counts the attestations that failed and links here; a signer the policy does not list gets the reason signer key id "<id>" is not in the trust policy (trust policy <file>) (for a certificate, signer "<subject>" (issuer "<issuer>") is not accepted by the policy (trust policy <file>); when the policy lists only keys the certificate is not verified, so the reason is certificate claiming signer "<subject>" (issuer "<issuer>") is not accepted by the policy: it lists no keyless identities (trust policy <file>)). For a verified result the text report adds signer: (key id, or subject and issuer, with the trust level name) and reference: lines. Errors joined from several causes print one aval: line per cause (an invalid aval.yaml); in a report (an invalid policy) the causes share the reason: line, separated by semicolons.

--record publishes a run record for statistics after the decision, for every outcome (see artifact-format.md). Records are unsigned, never read by aval run or aval verify, and never affect reuse or the exit code: a record that cannot be published is a warning.

--shadow verifies and runs the test anyway. If a verified result disagrees with the real run, that is a false hit: aval run prints aval: FALSE HIT: ... on stderr and exits 1. If they agree, it says reuse would have been correct.

Defense in depth for cacheability (invariant 7): a non-deterministic contract is a miss without any lookup, in aval run and aval verify, and so is an external-dependencies contract that the policy does not list in AllowedCacheability (routine non-reuse, not a security event). Also, a candidate whose signed test.cacheability differs from the local contract's is a verification failure, even if the policy would allow its class.

docs.title: Miss vs verification failure
docs.text:
These are different outcomes, in code and in exit codes:

Situation aval verify outcome Go error valid attestation, policy satisfied verified nil no attestation for this fingerprint miss wraps evidence.ErrNotFound only authentic attestations whose signer the policy lists below minTrustLevel miss CLI only (see Policy) attestation exists but fails signature or policy verification-failed wraps evidence.ErrVerification (*evidence.VerificationError carries the reason) Aval could not decide (registry down, I/O) error other

Each outcome has its own exit code; see the exit codes.

A miss is routine: inputs changed, nobody ran this yet. Run the test.

A verification failure is a security event. Someone published a result under this fingerprint that does not verify, or was signed by an identity the policy does not trust, or claims a different test id or fingerprint than the tag it sits under. Possible causes range from a misconfigured policy to a compromised publisher. The caller must run the test and surface the failure: fail the job, page, or at least emit a visible alert. Never collapse it into a silent re-run; doing so hides exactly the case the trust model exists to catch. That is why it has its own exit code (5) and its own outcome in aval verify --output json.

docs.title: Cacheability classes
docs.text:
Declared per test in aval.yaml (cacheability), copied into the predicate as test.cacheability. The contract (including this field) is hashed into the fingerprint, so a matching fingerprint implies the same declared class.

Class Meaning Reusable by default hermetic depends only on declared files and toolchain yes controlled-environment depends on declared services/images pinned in scope (e.g. compose file with digests) yes external-dependencies talks to things outside the scope (SaaS APIs, shared databases) no, only if the policy lists it in AllowedCacheability non-deterministic results vary across runs with identical inputs never

docs.title: Threats
docs.text: Threat Mitigation Compromised developer key Policy grants developer identities level 1 at most; CI sets MinTrustLevel >= 2, so a stolen developer key cannot satisfy CI. It can still poison that developer's own reuse. Prefer keyless (short-lived Fulcio certs, Rekor log) over long-lived keys. Tag swapping (sha256-<fp> repointed to another manifest) Tag is lookup only and must resolve to the fingerprint's deterministic anchor manifest; any other target is verification-failed. Candidates are the anchor's referrers, fetched and verified by digest. Replay of a passing result for a different fingerprint or test id Verify requires execution.fingerprint == ExpectedFingerprint and test.id == ExpectedTestID, both computed locally. The signed predicate cannot be re-labeled without breaking the signature. Mismatch is verification-failed. Undeclared input changed (file outside scope, unlisted env var, network service) Out of scope for detection in v0: the fingerprint only covers declared inputs. Mitigated by contract review, external-dependencies not being reusable by default and non-deterministic never being reusable, and the false-hit suite (roadmap item 4). Observed-input tracing is future work. Registry compromise (attacker can write arbitrary manifests and tags) Cannot forge signatures, so it cannot produce reuse on its own; injected attestations show up as verification-failed, or, when another candidate verifies, as a rejected entry with outcome verification-failed in the verify report (and an aval: SECURITY: ... line on stderr). It can delete attestations (forcing misses, i.e. re-runs) or deny service (error, re-run). Availability is out of scope. Forged or tampered run records (anyone with push access) Records are statistics, never evidence: unsigned, hung off a per-test stats anchor, and never fetched by aval run or aval verify, so they cannot cause reuse or count toward the candidate cap. A record crafted with a fingerprint anchor as its subject is filtered out by artifact type. They can skew statistics; treat them as informational. Dishonest but trusted signer (ran a modified test and signed "passed") Out of scope for Aval. A signature proves who claims it, not that the test ran honestly. Limit which identities get which level; level 3 (isolated) exists for this.

docs.title: Aval: vision
docs.text: Status: pre-alpha. Milestones 1 (contract + fingerprint) and 2 (sign, push and verify against a registry, aval run reuse or execute) are implemented.

docs.title: Thesis
docs.text:
Aval turns test results into signed, verifiable OCI artifacts. An expensive test runs once, locally or in CI. The result is published to an OCI registry as a signed attestation bound to a deterministic fingerprint of the test's inputs. Any other environment computes the same fingerprint, finds the attestation, verifies it, and if the trust policy allows it, reuses the result instead of running the test again.

This is not a test cache. It is a CI primitive: verifiable test execution reuse. A cache optimizes for hit rate and quietly tolerates a stale entry now and then. Aval optimizes for being able to justify every reuse, and when it can't, it runs the test.

A signature alone does not get you there. A signature proves who claims the test passed, not that it ran honestly or against the inputs you have now. Reuse is only safe when two things hold:

  • an explicit input contract (aval.yaml) that says what the test depends on, so "same inputs" is something you can check, and
  • a trust policy over signer identities, so "who ran it" is something you can accept or reject.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Heavy tests (integration, end-to-end, hardware, long suites) get re-run on every pipeline, branch and environment even when nothing they depend on has changed. Teams either pay for it in time and compute, or they skip tests based on informal judgment ("that service didn't change"), which nobody can audit. Existing build caches solve this for teams that buy into a hermetic build system. Most teams have not, and their CI cannot prove that a result from one environment is valid in another.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• A test contract (aval.yaml) that declares a test's identity, its runner command, its input scope, the environment conditions that matter, and its cacheability class.
  • A deterministic execution fingerprint over the declared inputs, independent of checkout path and file iteration order.
  • Signed in-toto attestations of execution results, stored in any OCI 1.1 registry and found by fingerprint.
  • Verification that keeps "no result" (miss) separate from "result exists but can't be trusted" (verification failure), in both code and exit codes.
  • A versioned output format and a public Go package (pkg/evidence) that other tools can consume without depending on Aval internals.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• No registry, server or database of our own. Storage, lookup and linking go through standard OCI registries.
  • No runtime tracing or input inference in v0. Scope is declared, not observed. Recording the files a test actually reads ("observed inputs") is future work, and would be used to check declared scope, not to replace it.
  • Not a build system and not a Bazel replacement. Aval doesn't model build graphs, actions or outputs. Teams already on Bazel's remote cache may not need it.
  • Not a test framework. Aval runs an arbitrary command and records its exit code. It doesn't discover, select or report individual test cases.
  • No knowledge of Pacto or any other consumer. Aval doesn't import Pacto or model its concepts. Consumers integrate through the stable formats below, and their adapters live in their own repositories.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text:
1. Standard supply-chain plumbing, no own infrastructure. Publishing and fetching use ORAS, signatures use Cosign/Sigstore, attestations use in-toto Statements in DSSE envelopes, and evidence is linked through OCI 1.1 referrers. Lookup goes only through the registry, via the tag sha256-<fingerprint hex>, and artifacts are always consumed by digest. Rationale: registries, signing and access control already exist and are already operated; tags are mutable, digests aren't.
  2. Scope belongs to the test contract, not the runner. Every test declares its inputs in aval.yaml (scope.source, scope.exclude, scope.dependencies, environment). Nothing is inferred or traced in v0. Rationale: the test author is the one who knows what the test depends on, and a declared scope can be reviewed in a PR.
  3. Fail closed. If input equivalence can't be proven, the test runs. That covers unknown contract fields, dependency globs that match nothing, symlinks in scope, and an empty scope. A miss (exit 4, ErrNotFound) and a verification failure (exit 5, ErrVerification) are separate outcomes. A verification failure is a security event and is never downgraded to a miss. Rationale: a false hit costs more than a re-run, and a forged or mis-signed result is something someone needs to look at.
  4. Trust tiers. Level 1 is a developer signature, meant as personal acceleration and not full trust. Level 2 is a runner with a verifiable identity. Level 3 is isolated execution with a verifiable attestation. The policy decides which signer identities are accepted, at which level, and the minimum level needed for reuse. With no policy, nothing is accepted. Rationale: how much a signed claim is worth depends on where it was produced, and that call belongs to whoever consumes the result.
  5. Test identity vs execution fingerprint. metadata.name / test.id says what is checked. The fingerprint says which concrete inputs and conditions a particular run had. Rationale: the same check gets many executions, and policy and reporting need to tell the two apart.
  6. Cacheability classes. hermetic and controlled-environment are reusable by default. external-dependencies needs an explicit policy opt-in. non-deterministic is never reusable. Rationale: a matching fingerprint only means something if the result depends on the declared inputs.
  7. Language-, framework- and CI-agnostic. v0 ships only a generic runner: an argv command with no shell interpolation, where the exit code is the result. Rationale: one generic runner covers every stack, and framework-specific runners can come later if there's demand.

docs.title: Consumption contract
docs.text:
External tools consume Aval results through:

  • versioned artifact and predicate formats with Aval's own media types (frozen: predicate type https://aval.trianalab.io/attestation/execution/v2, media type application/vnd.trianalab.aval.execution.v2+json, artifact type application/vnd.trianalab.aval.execution.v2, contract apiVersion aval.trianalab.io/v1),
  • neutral predicate fields: subject, test.id, result, execution.fingerprint, execution.environment, runner identity, startedAt/finishedAt, plus a free annotations map that Aval never reads,
  • the public Go package pkg/evidence (Parse, Verify),
  • aval verify --output json.

These formats are frozen; within a version they change additively only (see artifact-format.md).

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Bazel or a remote cache is already enough for some teams. Mitigation: don't compete there. Aval targets tests outside a hermetic build graph (integration, e2e, cross-environment). We'll know it isn't working if early users are mostly Bazel shops that also want Aval for build actions.
  • Declaring scope can cost more than it saves. Mitigation: keep the contract small (globs, lockfiles, a toolchain map) and make it debuggable with aval run --explain. Detection: contracts that drift away from the code they cover, or teams that give up on tests with a wide scope.
  • Real savings are small if inputs always change. If every commit touches the scope, the fingerprint never matches. Detection: the hit rate in the milestone 3 example and in early adopters' pipelines. A test whose scope is "the whole repo" is a bad fit, and the docs should say so.
  • Security policies may reject attestations from developer machines. Mitigation: this is expected, and it's why trust tiers exist. CI policies should require level 2 or higher, and level 1 stays personal acceleration. Detection: whether the value holds up when only runner and isolated signatures are accepted.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
1. Fingerprint + contract. Implemented. Exit criterion: aval.yaml is parsed and validated with unknown fields rejected, and aval run --fingerprint-only / --explain produce a deterministic aval-fingerprint/v1 digest and manifest that fail closed on undeclared or unprovable inputs.
  2. Push/verify against a local registry with Cosign signing. Implemented (aval run exits with the test's own result after a miss, and reports the miss). Exit criterion: aval run --push signs and publishes an attestation to a local OCI registry. aval verify and aval run against that registry reuse a policy-accepted result (exit 0), report a miss (exit 4), and report a tampered or untrusted attestation as a verification failure (exit 5). The policy file format is defined.
  3. End-to-end example in GitHub Actions. Exit criterion: a public example repo where one workflow run executes and publishes, a second run with unchanged inputs reuses the result, and a run with changed inputs misses and re-executes, all visible in the workflow logs. In progress: the example-go-compose job in .github/workflows/ci.yaml runs this story for examples/go-compose in this repository on every push to main (see its README). The release pipeline for signed aval binaries (checksums, SBOMs, SLSA provenance) is in place and dry-runs on every PR. The example and the dogfood shadow and publish jobs install the pinned release, verified before use. While the pin is v0.1.0, which cannot read the frozen aval.trianalab.io/v1 contracts, they build aval from the commit instead (#17). Aval also dogfoods itself (#28): ci-e2e runs the heavy suite (aval.e2e.yaml) through aval run and reuses a verified result, dogfood-shadow runs the unit suite (aval.yaml) with --shadow, and on main dogfood-publish signs and pushes both results to ghcr.io/trianalab/aval-attestations. A release requires a verified e2e attestation for its commit. See CONTRIBUTING.md.
  4. False-hit suite. Implemented. Exit criterion: an automated suite that applies every known kind of relevant change (source, dependency, toolchain, env var, exec bit, contract edit, symlink, file rename) and asserts that none of them can reuse a previous execution. The table-driven corpus in internal/fingerprint/corpus_test.go covers these kinds and pins the known gaps (see contract.md). The ci-false-hit CI job runs it on every PR and push, together with golden manifests of a fixed tree that fail on any change to them without an aval-fingerprint/vN bump (a mutation sweep of the manifest code found no manifest-changing mutant that passes; see contract.md). Committed goldens are append-only, so the golden cannot be rewritten instead.
  5. Stable consumption contract for external integrations. Exit criterion: the predicate type, media types, predicate fields, pkg/evidence API and aval verify --output json report are declared stable and versioned, with only additive changes allowed within v1, and an external consumer can verify results using pkg/evidence alone. In progress: the predicate type, media types, contract apiVersion and verify report version are frozen, with compatibility rules in artifact-format.md and golden files guarding the JSON shape (#17).

docs.title: How Aval works
docs.text:
Aval runs a test once, signs the result and stores it in your OCI registry. The next job with the same inputs checks that signature and skips the test.

flowchart LR
  run([aval run]) --> fp[fingerprint] --> look[look up] --> verify{trusted?}
  verify -- yes --> reuse([reuse]):::ok
  verify -- no --> exec[run the test] --> sign[sign] --> push([push]):::muted

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
1. Fingerprint. Aval reads aval.yaml, the test's contract. It hashes the contract and every file it lists into one fingerprint.
  2. Look up. Aval asks your registry for results stored under that fingerprint.
  3. Verify. Each result must carry a valid signature from a signer your policy trusts. See Trust.
  4. Reuse or run. A verified result is reused and the test does not run. Anything else runs the test. See Outcomes.
  5. Sign and push. With --push, Aval signs the new result and pushes it, so the next job can reuse it.

If Aval cannot prove that reuse is safe, the test runs.

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
A contract for a Go integration test, from the test contract:

apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1   # required, exact value
kind: Test                      # required, exact value

metadata:
  name: orders-integration      # test identity: WHAT is checked

runner:
  # argv, executed without a shell. Order matters and is part of the fingerprint.
  command: ["go", "test", "-tags=integration", "./orders/..."]

scope:
  source:                       # required, each glob must match >= 1 file
    - "orders/**/*.go"
    - "internal/**/*.go"
    - "testdata/orders/**"
  exclude:                      # optional, removes files selected by source
    - "**/*_bench_test.go"
  dependencies:                 # optional, each glob must match >= 1 file
    - "go.mod"
    - "go.sum"

environment:
  toolchain:                    # optional, declared, not detected (v0)
    go: "1.25"
  env:                          # optional, names only; values are hashed
    - CGO_ENABLED
    - GOFLAGS

cacheability: hermetic          # required, see "Cacheability classes"

The first job finds nothing, runs the test and pushes a signed result:

$ aval run --push --key keys/ci.pem --registry $REG --policy policy.yaml
miss orders-integration sha256:b40e9fac…
ran orders-integration: passed (exit 0)
pushed localhost:5055/acme/orders-aval@sha256:2496759a…

A second job with the same inputs reuses it:

$ aval run --registry $REG --policy policy.yaml
verified orders-integration sha256:b40e9fac…
reused passed result …/orders-aval@sha256:2496759a…

Change one file in scope and the fingerprint changes: the test runs again.

docs.title: What Aval does not do
docs.text:
• It does not guess inputs. A file the contract does not list is invisible to it.
  • It runs no server. Results live in an OCI registry you already have.

The full specs

These pages keep things short. The details are in the specs: the test contract, the trust model and the artifact format.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Each word Aval uses with a special meaning, defined once. Across the docs, hover a dotted word to see its short form.

docs.title: Attestation
docs.text: A signed statement: "test X, with inputs that hash to fingerprint F, produced result R". Aval stores it in your OCI registry. See the artifact format.

docs.title: Cacheability
docs.text: How safe a test is to reuse, declared in the contract. hermetic and controlled-environment are reusable. external-dependencies is reusable only if the policy allows it. non-deterministic is never reusable. See cacheability classes.

docs.title: Contract
docs.text: The aval.yaml file next to a test. It says what the test is, how to run it, and which inputs it reads. See the test contract.

docs.title: Fingerprint
docs.text: One sha256 hash of every input the contract declares: the contract itself (the command included), the files in scope, and the declared tool versions and environment variables. Same inputs, same fingerprint. See How Aval works.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The decision on a lookup: verified, miss, verification-failed or error. Only verified skips the test. See Outcomes.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text: A YAML file you write that lists the signers you trust and the trust level each one gets. Without a policy, nothing is reused. See Trust.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: The files the contract lists as test inputs: source files and dependencies such as go.mod. Aval sees nothing outside it. See what goes into the fingerprint.

docs.title: Signer
docs.text: The identity behind a signature: a CI job's OIDC identity (keyless), or a key. See Trust.

docs.title: Trust level
docs.text: How much the policy trusts a signer: 1 developer, 2 runner, 3 isolated. A result is reused only if its signer's level is at least the policy's minTrustLevel. See Trust.

docs.title: Outcomes
docs.text:
Every lookup ends in one of four outcomes. Only verified skips the test.

flowchart LR
  start([look up]) --> decide{could Aval<br>decide?}
  decide -- no --> error([error<br>exit 1]):::warn
  decide -- yes --> found{result<br>found?}
  found -- no --> miss([miss<br>exit 4]):::muted
  found -- yes --> valid{verifies?}
  valid -- yes --> verified([verified<br>exit 0]):::ok
  valid -- no --> failed([verification-failed<br>exit 5]):::err

The exit codes are those of aval verify. aval run turns every outcome except verified into a test run.

All exit codes, from the CLI reference:

Code aval run aval verify aval push 0 the test passed, or a verified passing result was reused a verified result exists (passing or failing) pushed 1 error (the test still runs when it can), or a false hit in --shadow error: registry, policy, trusted root or fingerprint error: signing, registry or a result that does not match the current inputs 2 bad flags or invalid aval.yaml bad flags or invalid aval.yaml bad flags or invalid aval.yaml 3 the test failed, or a verified failing result was reused not used not used 4 not used: a miss runs the test miss: no result the policy can reuse not used 5 verification failed, after running the test: a security event verification failed: a security event not used 6 reserved, never returned reserved, never returned reserved, never returned

A miss (4) is routine. A verification failure (5) means someone published a result the policy does not trust; never hide it or retry it away.

docs.title: The four outcomes
docs.text: Outcome What it means aval run does verified a trusted result exists for these exact inputs reuses it: exit 0 for a pass, 3 for a failure miss nothing to reuse: the inputs changed, or nobody ran them yet runs the test error Aval could not decide, such as a registry it cannot reach runs the test verification-failed a result exists but does not verify runs the test, then exits 5

docs.title: A miss is routine
docs.text:
You changed a file, so the fingerprint changed, so there is nothing to reuse yet. The test runs. This is the normal path for most pull requests.

A few other cases are also a miss: no --policy, a non-deterministic test, or a result signed below minTrustLevel.

docs.title: A verification failure is a security event
docs.text:
Someone pushed a result under your fingerprint that does not verify. The signature is bad, or the signer is not in your policy, or the result claims other inputs. The cause can be a wrong policy or an attacker.

Aval runs the test, prints aval: SECURITY: ... and exits 5. Do not hide it and do not retry it away: fail the job and look.

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
$ aval verify --registry $REG --policy policy.yaml
miss orders-integration sha256:b40e9fac…
reason: registry.Lookup …: no attestation found for fingerprint
$ echo $?
4

In a script, branch on the exit code:

aval verify --registry "$REG" --policy policy.yaml
case $? in
  0) echo "a trusted result exists" ;;
  4) echo "miss: the test must run" ;;
  5) echo "SECURITY: a result failed verification" >&2; exit 1 ;;
  *) echo "error: the test must run" ;;
esac

The full spec

The JSON report is in the artifact format, the commands in the CLI reference.

docs.title: Trust
docs.text:
A signed result is reused only if your policy trusts the signer. The result cannot vouch for itself.

flowchart LR
  ci[CI job] --> r[signed result]
  dev[developer key] --> r
  r --> sig{valid<br>signature?}
  sig -- no --> fail([verification-failed<br>exit 5]):::err
  sig -- yes --> who{signer in<br>the policy?}
  who -- no --> fail
  who -- yes --> lvl{level high<br>enough?}
  lvl -- no --> miss([miss<br>exit 4]):::muted
  lvl -- yes --> ok([verified<br>reuse]):::ok

All exit codes, from the CLI reference:

Code aval run aval verify aval push 0 the test passed, or a verified passing result was reused a verified result exists (passing or failing) pushed 1 error (the test still runs when it can), or a false hit in --shadow error: registry, policy, trusted root or fingerprint error: signing, registry or a result that does not match the current inputs 2 bad flags or invalid aval.yaml bad flags or invalid aval.yaml bad flags or invalid aval.yaml 3 the test failed, or a verified failing result was reused not used not used 4 not used: a miss runs the test miss: no result the policy can reuse not used 5 verification failed, after running the test: a security event verification failed: a security event not used 6 reserved, never returned reserved, never returned reserved, never returned

A miss (4) is routine. A verification failure (5) means someone published a result the policy does not trust; never hide it or retry it away.

docs.title: Signers
docs.text:
A signer is who signed a result. There are two kinds:

  • A CI job (keyless). The job signs with a short-lived certificate from Sigstore, tied to its OIDC identity, such as one GitHub Actions workflow on main.
  • A key. A developer signs with a local key file.

docs.title: Trust levels
docs.text:
Your policy gives each signer a trust level:

Level Name Constant Who Good for 0 unknown TrustUnknown level could not be established never accepted 1 developer TrustDeveloper a developer's local signature personal acceleration only: skip a test you already ran on your machine. Not full trust. 2 runner TrustRunner a CI runner with a verifiable workload identity (e.g. GitHub Actions OIDC) reuse in CI. CI should require at least this level. 3 isolated TrustIsolated an isolated execution with a verifiable attestation of the environment itself reuse where the runner host is not trusted either

The predicate inside a result also claims a level. Aval ignores that claim: the level always comes from your policy.

docs.title: The policy
docs.text:
A policy is a YAML file you keep in your repository. This one trusts the main branch workflow for CI reuse, and Alice's key at developer level:

apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Policy
minTrustLevel: runner           # developer | runner | isolated
# trustedRoot: sigstore/trusted_root.json  # keyless only; default: Sigstore public-good, fetched with TUF
identities:
  - issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
    subjectRegexp: https://github\.com/acme/orders/\.github/workflows/ci\.yaml@refs/heads/main
    trustLevel: runner
  - publicKey: keys/alice.pub   # PEM public key file
    trustLevel: developer
allowedCacheability: [external-dependencies]

With minTrustLevel: runner, a result Alice signed is a miss: the test runs. Without --policy, nothing is trusted and every test runs.

docs.title: What a signature proves
docs.text:
• Proves: who signed the result, and that nobody changed it since.
  • Does not prove: that the test ran honestly, or that inputs outside the contract were the same.

So only grant a level to signers you would trust to run the test yourself.

The full spec

The trust model covers keyless verification, the policy fields and the threats Aval defends against.

docs.title: Use Aval in GitHub Actions
docs.text:
Goal: a workflow on main that reuses a verified test result, or runs the test and publishes a signed one.

flowchart LR
  job([push to main]) --> run[aval run]
  run -- verified --> skip([test skipped]):::ok
  run -- anything else --> test[test runs] --> push[aval push] --> reg([GHCR]):::muted

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
These are the steps of the example-go-compose job in Aval's own ci.yaml. They run on every push to main. Copy them into your job and set three variables: REPO (your registry repository), CONTRACT (your aval.yaml) and POLICY (your trust policy).

The job needs these permissions:

    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
      id-token: write

The steps log in to GHCR, run the test or reuse the result, and publish a new result signed with the workflow's identity:

      - name: Log in to GHCR
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          echo "$GH_TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io -u "$GITHUB_ACTOR" --password-stdin
          echo "| step | outcome |" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          echo "|---|---|" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
      - name: Publish (runs and pushes unless a verified result exists)
        run: |
          aval run -f "$CONTRACT" --registry "$REPO" --policy "$POLICY" --report publish.json
          if [ "$(jq -r .outcome publish.json)" != "verified" ]; then
            # The Actions OIDC token for Fulcio, fetched after the test so a
            # slow test cannot outlive it. aval push reads SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN.
            SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN=$(curl -fsS -H "Authorization: bearer $ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN" \
              "$ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL&audience=sigstore" | jq -r .value)
            export SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN
            aval push -f "$CONTRACT" --registry "$REPO"
          fi
          echo "| publish | \`$(jq -r .outcome publish.json)\` |" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

Install aval in an earlier step with the installer.

docs.title: What happens
docs.text:
1. aval run fingerprints the inputs and looks in REPO.
  2. If a trusted result exists, the test does not run (outcome verified).
  3. Otherwise the test runs. The step then asks GitHub for an OIDC token and aval push signs the result with it and publishes it.
  4. If the test fails (exit 3) or a result does not verify (exit 5), the step fails and nothing is pushed.

The policy for this job trusts only this workflow on main:

# Trust policy for the GitHub Actions demo (the example-go-compose job in
# .github/workflows/ci.yaml): reuse only results signed keyless by that
# workflow on main. Anything else that sits under the fingerprint, such as a
# result signed with some key, is a verification failure (exit 5).
apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Policy
minTrustLevel: runner
identities:
  - issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
    subjectRegexp: https://github\.com/TrianaLab/aval/\.github/workflows/ci\.yaml@refs/heads/main
    trustLevel: runner
Why the token is fetched after the test

The OIDC token is short-lived. Fetching it after the test means a slow test cannot outlive it. aval push reads it from $SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN; runner.command never sees it.

Pull requests

packages: write and id-token: write are write scopes, so this job runs only on push to main. A pull request job can still reuse: give it contents: read, run aval run with --registry and --policy, and leave out the push. GHCR packages that are public can be read without a login.

Fail on a security event

aval run exits 5 when a result under your fingerprint does not verify. Do not add || true around it. See Outcomes.

docs.title: Consume evidence from Go
docs.text:
Goal: check an Aval result from your own Go program with pkg/evidence, and tell a miss from a security event.

flowchart LR
  fetch([envelope, fetched by digest]) --> check[evidence.Verify]
  check -- ok --> p([predicate]):::ok
  check -- ErrVerification --> alert([alert, do not reuse]):::err
  none([nothing found]) --> miss([ErrNotFound: run the test]):::muted

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
Add the module:

go get github.com/TrianaLab/aval@latest

This is Check from examples/evidence-consumer, a separate module that imports only pkg/evidence. CI builds and tests it:

// Check returns the verified predicate of a DSSE envelope fetched by digest.
// nil envBytes means the lookup found nothing: evidence.ErrNotFound, a miss.
// Every other failure wraps evidence.ErrVerification, a security event. The
// caller runs the test unless Check returns a passed predicate.
func Check(ctx context.Context, envBytes []byte, opts evidence.VerifyOptions) (*evidence.Predicate, error) {
    if envBytes == nil {
        return nil, evidence.ErrNotFound
    }
    var env evidence.Envelope
    if err := json.Unmarshal(envBytes, &env); err != nil {
        return nil, &evidence.VerificationError{Reason: "decoding envelope: " + err.Error()}
    }
    v, err := evidence.Verify(ctx, &env, opts)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return v.Predicate, nil
}

Branch on what it returns, with errors.Is:

Check returns Meaning Do a predicate with Result == evidence.ResultPassed a trusted pass for these inputs reuse it evidence.ErrNotFound nothing to reuse: a miss run the test evidence.ErrVerification a result that does not verify alert, run the test, do not reuse a predicate with another Result a trusted failure for these inputs treat the test as failed

docs.title: What you bring
docs.text:
• The envelope bytes. Fetch them by digest with ORAS or any registry client. The layout is in Artifact format.
  • A SignatureVerifier. pkg/evidence checks the policy, not the cryptography. The example brings an ed25519 one; a Sigstore one for consumers is planned for milestone 5.
  • The identities. Build them from your own policy. Trust never comes from the predicate.
Read an aval verify report instead

If you run aval verify --output json, read its report with evidence.Report. The example's Reuse function does this and fails closed on any verification-failed candidate.

Compatibility

pkg/evidence changes additively within a major version. A test compares its exported API with a committed snapshot. See Go API compatibility.

docs.title: Measure reuse
docs.text:
Goal: find out how often Aval would reuse a result, and whether reuse would have been right, before you let it skip any test.

flowchart LR
  run([aval run --shadow]) --> v[verify] --> t[run the test anyway]
  t --> same{same result?}
  same -- yes --> ok([reuse would be correct]):::ok
  same -- no --> fh([FALSE HIT, exit 1]):::err
  t --> rec([run record in the registry]):::muted

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
Run in shadow mode and record every run:

aval run --shadow --record --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval --policy policy.yaml

--shadow verifies as usual, then runs the test anyway. If a verified result exists and agrees with the run, Aval prints shadow: reuse of <reference> would have been correct. If it disagrees, Aval prints aval: FALSE HIT: ... and exits 1. A false hit usually means the contract misses an input: fix the scope before you turn shadow mode off.

--record publishes one run record per run. A record looks like this:

{
  "version": "aval.trianalab.io/run-record/v1",
  "testId": "orders-integration",
  "fingerprint": "sha256:3f9a7c2e1b4d5f60718293a4b5c6d7e8f9012a3b4c5d6e7f8091a2b3c4d5e6f7",
  "outcome": "verified",
  "reused": true,
  "result": "passed",
  "testDurationMs": 0,
  "savedDurationMs": 1184000,
  "avalVersion": "0.3.0",
  "recordedAt": "2026-11-06T09:00:00Z",
  "ciRunUrl": "https://ci.example.com/acme/orders/runs/42"
}

docs.title: Record from where you can write
docs.text:
Same jobSeparate job

The job that runs the test has write access to the registry:

aval run --record --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval --policy policy.yaml

The test job writes the record to a file. A job with write access, which runs no tests, publishes it:

aval run --record-file record.json --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval --policy policy.yaml
aval record --record-file record.json --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval

Aval's own CI does this on main for its end-to-end suite.

docs.title: Read the numbers
docs.text:
aval stats, which sums the records of a test into a table of hits, misses and time saved, is in progress in #88. Until it lands, list the records yourself:

List run records with ORAS

Records hang off the tag stats-<test id>:

oras discover --artifact-type application/vnd.trianalab.aval.run.v1 ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval:stats-orders-integration
Records are statistics, not evidence

Records are unsigned. aval run and aval verify never read them, so a forged record cannot cause reuse. Recording is best-effort: a record that cannot be published prints aval: warning: run record not published and never changes the exit code.

What the fields mean

reused is true when the test did not run. savedDurationMs is how long the reused run took when it was recorded. With --shadow, reused is always false. Every field is in Artifact format: run records.

docs.title: Sign with a key or keyless
docs.text:
Goal: sign a test result so that others can check who published it.

flowchart LR
  run([aval run]) --> result[.aval/result.json] --> push[aval push]
  push -- key file --> keyed([key-based]):::muted
  push -- OIDC token --> keyless([keyless]):::ok

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
KeyKeyless

Make a P-256 key and a policy that trusts it:

openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out aval.key
openssl pkey -in aval.key -pubout -out aval.pub
cat > policy.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Policy
minTrustLevel: developer
identities:
  - publicKey: aval.pub
    trustLevel: developer
EOF

Run the test, then sign and push the result:

aval run --push --key aval.key --registry localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval

This is the quickstart path; a test runs it as written.

Put an OIDC token in $SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN and leave out --key:

export SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN="<OIDC token for audience sigstore>"
aval run --push --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval

On GitHub Actions the job gets the token itself; see Use Aval in GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Which one
docs.text:
Key Keyless Who signs whoever holds the key file a CI workload or a person, proven by an OIDC token Policy entry publicKey: aval.pub issuer and subjectRegexp Typical trust level developer runner Needs network to verify no yes, unless the policy pins trustedRoot

Use keyless in CI. Use a key on your laptop or in a closed network.

Which keys work

Aval signs with an unencrypted ECDSA P-256 private key in PEM (PKCS#8 or SEC1). Cosign keys are encrypted and do not work. Make one with openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out aval.key.

Sign later with aval push

aval run records the result in .aval/result.json. aval push signs and publishes it later, with the same --key or token. It refuses a result whose inputs no longer match the contract:

aval run --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval --policy policy.yaml
aval push --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval
What a signature proves

A signature proves who published the result, not that the test ran honestly. That is why the policy decides how much each signer is trusted. See Trust.

docs.text:
Goal: go from an exit code or an error message to its cause and its fix.

aval verify --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval --policy policy.yaml; echo "exit $?"

docs.title: Write a trust policy
docs.text:
Goal: a policy.yaml that says whose results you reuse, and nobody else's.

flowchart LR
  r([a result]) --> sig{valid signature?}
  sig -- no --> f([verification-failed]):::err
  sig -- yes --> who{signer in policy?}
  who -- no --> f
  who -- yes --> lvl{level high enough?}
  lvl -- no --> m([miss]):::muted
  lvl -- yes --> ok([verified]):::ok

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
Keyless (CI)Key

Trust one GitHub Actions workflow on main. This is the policy of the example-go-compose job in Aval's CI:

# Trust policy for the GitHub Actions demo (the example-go-compose job in
# .github/workflows/ci.yaml): reuse only results signed keyless by that
# workflow on main. Anything else that sits under the fingerprint, such as a
# result signed with some key, is a verification failure (exit 5).
apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Policy
minTrustLevel: runner
identities:
  - issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
    subjectRegexp: https://github\.com/TrianaLab/aval/\.github/workflows/ci\.yaml@refs/heads/main
    trustLevel: runner

Trust one key file. This is the README quickstart, which a test runs:

openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out aval.key
openssl pkey -in aval.key -pubout -out aval.pub
cat > policy.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Policy
minTrustLevel: developer
identities:
  - publicKey: aval.pub
    trustLevel: developer
EOF

Use it with --policy:

aval verify --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval --policy policy.yaml

Without --policy, Aval trusts nobody and the test always runs.

docs.title: The fields
docs.text: Field What it does identities the signers you accept: an issuer plus a subjectRegexp, or a publicKey file trustLevel how much you trust that signer: developer, runner or isolated minTrustLevel the lowest level you reuse; a signer below it is a miss allowedCacheability optional: add external-dependencies to reuse those tests too trustedRoot optional: a pinned Sigstore root, so keyless checks need no network

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Anchor the subject to one workflow file and one branch. A pull request branch can run any code, so do not trust it at runner level.
  • Give developer keys developer and keep minTrustLevel: runner in CI. A laptop policy with minTrustLevel: developer then reuses results signed with those keys, and CI never does.
  • Levels come from the policy only. What a result says about itself is never trusted.
How the subject is matched

subjectRegexp must match the whole subject, as if it started with ^ and ended with $. Escape dots: github\.com. For GitHub Actions the subject is https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/<workflow path>@<ref>.

Keyless checks and the network

A keyless policy fetches the Sigstore trusted root on first use and caches it under $HOME/.sigstore. Offline, that candidate is an error and the test runs. Pin the root with trustedRoot to avoid this; see the trust model.

What Aval rejects

Unknown fields, a missing level, no identities, an identity with both publicKey and issuer, and non-deterministic in allowedCacheability. The error names the field; see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Write a contract
docs.text:
Goal: an aval.yaml that lists every input of your test, so a result is reused only when none of them changed.

flowchart LR
  c([aval.yaml]) --> s[scope: files the test reads] --> fp[fingerprint]
  c --> k[cacheability: how safe reuse is] --> d{reusable?}
  fp --> d

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
This contract runs a Go integration test against Redis from Docker Compose. It is examples/go-compose/aval.yaml, which CI runs:

apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Test
metadata:
  name: counter-integration
runner:
  command: ["sh", "-c", "docker compose up -d --wait && REDIS_ADDR=localhost:16379 go test -tags=integration -count=1 ./...; rc=$?; docker compose down; exit $rc"]
scope:
  source: ["**/*.go", "compose.yaml"]
  dependencies: [go.mod]
environment:
  toolchain: {go: "1.25"}
cacheability: controlled-environment

Put it next to your test and check what it hashes:

aval run --explain --fingerprint-only

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Name the test. metadata.name says what is checked. It stays the same when the inputs change.
  2. Say how to run it. runner.command is an argv list. Aval does not use a shell unless you call one, like the example does.
  3. List the inputs. scope.source lists the files the test reads. scope.dependencies lists lockfiles. Globs are relative to the contract's directory; ** matches any number of directories.
  4. Pick a cacheability class. It tells Aval and the policy how safe reuse is.
Class Use it when Reused hermetic the test reads only the declared files yes controlled-environment it uses services you pin, such as a Compose image by digest yes external-dependencies it calls something you do not control only if the policy allows it non-deterministic the same inputs can give a different result never

docs.title: Check the scope
docs.text:
--explain prints every file, toolchain entry and variable that went into the fingerprint. A file that is not listed is not an input: changing it does not change the fingerprint. If the test reads it, add it to scope.

What --explain prints

Globs that match nothing

Every glob in source and dependencies must match at least one file. Otherwise Aval cannot fingerprint, and the test always runs. exclude globs may match nothing.

Environment

environment.toolchain records versions, such as go: "1.25". Aval does not check them. environment.env names variables whose values go into the fingerprint.
